Description: This chef built his menu through careful study of how classic recipes work. He pours his passion into such traditional dishes as pâté en croûte and pigeon pie. Blending French tradition with a modern sensibility, with a light touch on the seasoning. Also skilled in game, his wild hare royale, winner of an international competition, is available by reservation only. As dishes are served in double portions, bookings require a minimum of two guests.

Name: à terre
Description: Set in the shadow of the Royal Danish Theatre, this small, intimate restaurant was founded on family and friendship. While the narrative behind the menu may have evolved recently, the restaurant’s ambition remains the same: to create a space where guests can escape and forget about the world outside. French recipes form the base of the cooking but take their inspiration from Nordic ingredients. Choose between the set Signature Menu or the shorter Menu Essentiel if you’re planning a trip the theatre as well; you’ll find delights such as pollock on fried bread and stuffed quail with sherry sauce.

Name: âme
Description: The aim of this unusual bistro, run by business partners Pachi Rodríguez (manning the stove) and Joey Attieh (as sommelier), is to pay continued homage to French cuisine, while at the same time making full use of seasonal local ingredients (artichokes from Prat, red prawns from Palamós, trout and acorn-fed duck from the Pyrenees, etc.). The dynamic and constantly evolving cuisine only sees the light through two tasting menus (Experiencia and Epicúreo) that propose a journey through the flavours of the Mediterranean from the perspective of French cuisine. Their delicious Montseny maitake with cashew nuts and foie is a very special dish.

Name: çayca
Description: A once-in-a-lifetime experience, welcomed by a tea practitioner and a patissière. The meal begins with a cup of matcha, imbibed while watching a simple tea ceremony. ‘Dessert a l'assiette’, works of patisserie art on a plate, are patiently assembled one-by-one before your eyes. In the manner of French confectionary, recipes are layers of many elements. The sweetness of fruit, the tartness of citrus and vinegar, and contrasting textures are gathered on one plate. The interior, a fusion of tearoom and Western-style house, is altogether novel.

Name: épa
Description: His love of classical cuisine led the chef to explore traditional techniques. At the same time, he studied avant-garde French cooking to keep pace with the times. The courses reflects both a respect for the classics and a willingness to tackle the modern. Contemporary-style amuse-bouche and starters give way to classic pastry-wrapped fish and meat dishes. Diners can enjoy a relaxed meal in a homely setting with Nordic furnishings.

Name: étsi - l'ouzeri
Description: Saganaki cheese, gyro merida, myzithropita (cheesecake), spanakopita – the menu gives it away: this is French-Greek chef Mikaela Liaroutsos's new Greek taverna, and it's just a stone's throw from the original restaurant that made her name. The food is served as a series of mezes, to savour as you dream of Greek holidays, past or future. The traditional songs playing in the background might tempt you to pull out a sirtaki step after a glass of ouzo.

Name: étsi - le bistro
Description: Mikaela Liaroutsos, a young chef of Greek origin, has returned to the cuisine of her childhood, after learning the ropes in some prestigious establishments. She rolls out strikingly fresh mezze designed for sharing – marinated sea bream, capers, Aleppo pepper and some first-rate scallops with pistachio butter, mizithra cheese and tarragon. The feta, olives, capers, charcuterie, cheese, olive oil and wines – all imported directly from Greece – are enjoyed in a relaxed space.

Name: Ăn Ði
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Interesting wine list,Pets not allowed
Description: Modern Vietnamese food from a chef trained in French cuisine. Ăn Ði combines seasonal Japanese ingredients with bánh xèo, raw spring rolls and phở to express the four seasons of Japan with Vietnamese cuisine. With a skilled sommelier at the helm, you can also expect perfect pairings that elevate each dish. The emphasis is on wines, but the restaurant also showcases a modern approach to pairing sake and shochu. The restaurant name means '’Bon appétit!’ in Vietnamese.

Name: Đông Phố
Address: 57 Ho Xuan Huong Street, Xuan Hoa Ward, Ho Chi Minh City, 72407, Vietnam
Description: Popular among the locals and tourists alike, this unpretentious eatery shares a bungalow with an ice cream parlour and specialises in traditional Vietnamese dishes and French snacks. If you find the vast menu a bit daunting, the tasting menu is a great way to sample all the signature dishes. Try the assorted spring rolls, featuring a delightful variety of types on one plate, each filled with unique ingredients and crafted in different styles.

Name: İsabey Bağevi
Address: Gölcükler Mahallesi, 901. Sokak İstasyon Mevkii No:38, Menderes, Izmir, 35470, Türkiye
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Pets allowed only in outdoor dining areas (patio/terrace),Terrace
Description: The Isabey wine estate grows mostly Sauvignon Blanc, but you will find more than impressive rows of vines on its land. Indeed, there is a magnificent terrace on which to dine in the shade of a majestic plane tree that is over 350 years old. This restaurant is committed to serving food and wine of the highest quality. The buttery lamb stock with medium-rare lamb chops and the squid stuffed with minced lamb and accompanied by a fine white wine sauce are testament to the depth and flavour of this classic cuisine.

Name: Łaskawość Tytusa
Description: In both its sleek, minimalistic design and its globetrotting culinary influences, this feels like the epitome of the contemporary bistro. Although there are some traditional Polish elements on the concise menu, expect flavours from the Mediterranean and Levant too. The fresh, colourful dishes are full of contrasting flavours and textures – such as the pan-fried oyster mushrooms with maple syrup and chilli on a bed of labneh with dill and hazelnut.

Name: Ōre
Address: 11/31 Sathu Pradit Road, Chong Nonsi, Yan Nawa, Bangkok, 10120, Thailand
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Counter dining,Pets not allowed
Description: (The restaurant is temporarily closed.) Ōre, with its minimalist design of wood, fabric and natural tones, offers an intimate culinary journey of over 30 bite-sized creations centred on Thai ingredients with select imports. The chef extols the flavour-enhancing properties of the mineral water that he gets shipped in from a spring near Sai Yok Waterfall to use in his cooking. His creative dishes highlight natural flavours and aromas that deepen throughout the meal, making for an unforgettable dining experience.

Name: Śląska Prohibicja
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Pets allowed only in outdoor dining areas (patio/terrace),Terrace
Description: In the history-rich neighbourhood of Nikiszowiec, this large restaurant sits on the ground floor of what was once accommodation for local miners. In fact, you can still get a sense of the vintage canteen the dining room once was. Today, it’s enlivened by bookshelves and foliage, while the cooking offers hearty renditions of Polish and Silesian classics. A prime example is the breaded bone-in pork chop with piquant dried capers, cucumber salad and sour cream.

Name: Şans Restaurant
Address: Hacı Adil Caddesi, Palmiye Sokak No:1, Levent/Beşiktaş, Istanbul, 34330, Türkiye
Description: This elegantly appointed villa has been a favourite destination for business clientele since 1992. They come for the attentive service, private dining options and expert wine recommendations (be sure to try one of the Turkish reds!). But the principal draw is undoubtedly the cuisine: a fusion of authentic Turkish flavours and Mediterranean influences. From steaming cheese dumplings to a creamy mushroom risotto and slow-cooked lamb neck with barbecued vegetables: generosity is always on the menu here. A firm favourite with many foodies.

Name: Špacapanova Hiša
Description: Since 1937, Casa Špacapan has been a point of reference for the cuisine of the Karst. Today, under the direction of Ago Špacapan, the offering is renewed in the spirit of quality and territory. The kitchen celebrates local produce, much of it from their own production: charcuterie and cheeses aged in the cellar, estate wines (Teran, Rebula, Malvazija…), vegetables from the kitchen garden, and ingredients from trusted small suppliers. The dishes tell the story of the Karst, with specialities such as roast lamb or kid and ravioli filled with fresh cow’s curd. Alongside the à la carte and tasting menus, a truffle-dedicated menu has recently been introduced. The cellar, overseen by Miro Špacapan, Ago’s father, completes the experience with wines, vinegars and artisan distillates.

Name: Šug
Description: “Šug” in Croatian means sauce, a central element in the chef’s cooking. Away from the crowds of the city centre, this is an informal and relaxed venue for enjoying generous dishes of Dalmatian tradition, land and sea, with some Italian influences. The kitchen celebrates simple and authentic Mediterranean ingredients that tell the story of the flavours and traditions of the local area. The restaurant occupies a small stone tavern of warm and pleasant character, with a pretty outdoor patio for the summertime.

Name: Źródło
Description: Fun, colourful and with an infectiously positive vibe, it’s easy to see why this wine bar and bistro is so popular – and booking is essential if you want to sample the kitchen’s soul-warming comfort food. The likes of pan-fried zander with beurre blanc and trout roe are a prime example of everything this place is about: big portions of unpretentious, flavour-driven cooking. The intriguing, on-trend wine list includes organic, biodynamic and orange options available by the glass.

Name: Ốc Dì Tú
Address: 144C Quan Thanh Street, Ba Dinh Ward, Hanoi, 100000, Vietnam
Description: Vietnamese for snail, Ốc is the focus of this simple eatery with pila polita, tiger moon, shark eye and canarium snails on the menu. The large melo melo, the tastiest, is grilled until soft and served with scallions and fried garlic; the price depends on its size. The rich variety of seafood options includes prawns, Halong squid, Venus clams and blood cockles. The steamed Venus clams with lemongrass, chilli and pineapple exude a deep umami flavour.

Name: Ốc Oanh
Address: 534 Vinh Khanh Street, Khanh Hoi Ward, Ho Chi Minh City, 754000, Vietnam
Description: This joint on a busy street serves a range of seafood cooked in countless ways. Whelks, tiger prawns, lobster, octopus, crab… the choice is yours. The authentic outdoor vibe more than makes up for the lack of air conditioning.

Name: Ốc Vi Saigon
Address: 21 Gia Ngu Street, Hoan Kiem Ward, Hanoi, 100000, Vietnam
Description: The extensive, reasonably priced menu is mainly composed of seafood dishes with a wide array of shellfish from oysters to white clams, snails, cockles and scallops. Snails are the specialty here, cooked in a variety of ways and sauces. The stir-fried white clams in garlic butter exude a strong aroma, while an irresistible umami flavour pervades the stir-fried cockles with tamarind. Order a mini baguette so you can mop up the delicious sauce!

Name: Ốc Đào (Cầu Ông Lãnh)
Address: 212B/D48 Nguyen Trai Street, Cau Ong Lanh Ward, Ho Chi Minh City, 71014, Vietnam
Description: Spread over three floors, this medium-sized seafood restaurant is clean and well organised, with air-conditioning on the second floor. Shellfish takes centre stage, with plenty of fresh options on offer. The cooking is straightforward but effective, especially the garlic-butter sautéed and salt-grilled dishes, which allow the natural flavours to shine. Most items are priced on the menu, while premium seafood from the tanks is available at market price. Do remember to bring cash.

Name: “8” By Andrew Sheridan
Address: 16 Cook Street, Liverpool, L2 9RF, United Kingdom
Description: It was something of a homecoming for eponymous Chef Andrew Sheridan when he relocated his immersive restaurant from Birmingham to this Victorian property in central Liverpool. Guests gather in the dimly lit lounge for drinks and precisely made snacks, before heading downstairs to one of the two eight-seater counters, each with its own chef. They cook and explain their complex, ambitious dishes in front of the guests, with influences from around the globe helping them to showcase bold, distinct flavours underpinned by high-quality produce.
